title: How to Learn from Games Without Copying Them | 3 Steps to Analyze Fun

scenes.title: Why similar features feel different
lines: You recreate movement and jumping from a game you love, but playing your version feels unexpectedly different.
You may have transferred visible features while missing what players noticed and decided.
Jumps in Super Meat Boy, dashes in Hollow Knight, and movement through portals all involve different decisions.
Let us observe small actions, change their conditions, and build rules for our own game.

scenes.title: Observe one action
lines: First, break an enjoyable moment into a small action. Go beyond saying that it looks beautiful or feels good.
Before a jump, you read the platform and gap. In the air, you adjust your landing. After landing, you check the result.
Write down noticing, choosing, acting, and recognizing the outcome. This gives your analysis a clear target.
In Hollow Knight, examine when and where a dash is used, and where it leaves the player. Copying a character color does not reproduce those decisions.

scenes.title: Describe conditions behind a feeling
lines: Second, turn a feeling into conditions you can examine. Saying that a dash feels exciting does not specify what to build.
Is it the speed, passing through danger, or being able to try again quickly? The same action may be enjoyable for several reasons.
Portal is more than an effect showing someone entering a doorway. You consider where entrances and exits should go to move yourself and objects.
These examples are comparisons for describing decisions, risks, and outcomes more precisely. They are not ready-made answers for your own game.

scenes.title: Change one condition
lines: Now change one condition at a time in an original prototype. Keep the jump and platforms alike, but make the landing zone wide on one side and narrow on the other.
Both versions use a jump button, but the narrow landing asks for more attention to timing and adjustment. Keeping other conditions alike makes comparison easier.
Next, compare immediate retries with a brief wait after failure. Does the change help players learn the rule, or simply add waiting?
Changing speed, artwork, and rewards together makes their effects hard to separate. A small test should first help you examine an idea.

scenes.title: Recombine a decision
lines: Third, choose a decision you want to preserve and combine it with different rules. Imagine enjoying the decision to wait briefly before crossing a gap.
That decision could also appear in a puzzle about passing through a moving doorway or a stealth activity that permits movement during a signal.
Our three prototypes reuse simple shapes for jumping, crossing, and moving. Different signals and restart positions produce different choices.
These prototypes are not proven to be fun. Ask playtesters what they watched and when they intended to act, then revise the rules.

scenes.title: Record play, not just features
lines: When analyzing a game, record one play sequence rather than only a feature list. What did you notice, choose, and use to recognize the result?
Change one condition, then put the decision you want to keep into a new situation. Check whether your explanation holds up in a playable test.
Understanding the experience behind a finished design can help you more than transferring its finished solution.
Choose one recent moment you enjoyed. Start with the decision you made, and turn it into a small test.
